Morning routines in a new language

Every morning Mara wakes up at half past six and opens the window of her small flat. The street below is still quiet, and the first tram of the day rattles past the bakery on the corner. She makes coffee, sits down at the kitchen table and reads one page of a novel in the language she is learning. One page is not much, but it is every single day, and that is the part that matters.

At first she understood almost nothing. She wrote down every unknown word, and the list grew faster than her memory. After a few weeks she changed the rule: only three words a day, chosen because they appeared again and again. The list became short, and the words began to stay.

Her teacher used to say that a language is not a wall of grammar but a road of habits. You walk it in small steps, and you notice the distance only when you look back. Mara did not believe that in the beginning. She believed it on the morning when she understood a joke on the radio, laughed, and only afterwards realised that nobody had translated anything for her.

In the evening she speaks for ten minutes with a neighbour who moved to the city two years ago. They talk about the weather, about the price of vegetables, about a film neither of them has finished watching. The conversations are simple and full of mistakes, and both of them keep going anyway.

On Sunday she reads a longer text and writes five sentences about it. She reads the sentences aloud twice: once slowly, once at the speed of ordinary speech. Then she closes the notebook and does something else entirely, because a language that never leaves the desk never becomes a language at all.
